current.title: Account takeover
current.what: Account takeover is when someone other than the customer gets into an existing account and uses it. Public descriptions of the pattern usually point to stolen passwords, phishing, credential stuffing, SIM swap, or malware, followed by a change to the phone, email, address, or payout destination.
redFlags: A login from a new device or an unusual network, then a contact or payout change in the same session
A password or multi-factor reset immediately before a new payee, shipping address, or phone number
Many failed sign-ins, then one success, on accounts that share a device or IP address
Profile changes clustered with a payment, transfer, or high-risk order
protect: Use a different password for every account. A password manager makes this practical.
Turn on multi-factor authentication, ideally an authenticator app or passkey instead of text messages.
Never share a one-time code. Your bank or a real company will not call or text asking for one.
Ask your mobile carrier for a port-out PIN or SIM lock to make SIM swaps harder.
Turn on login and account-change alerts, and act quickly on any you don't recognize.
detect: Join login events (time, IP, device) to account-change and payment events on the same customer
Look for short sequences: failed logins, a success, a contact change, then a payment
Compare the session with that customer's usual device, network, and time of day
Group attempts that share a device or IP across many accounts, which is the shape of credential stuffing
Review velocity of password resets and authenticator changes before money movement
